q: What is ACP cladding, and is it good for Kerala's climate?
a:
ACP (aluminium composite panel) is two thin aluminium sheets bonded to a core. It is fixed on an aluminium frame in front of your wall to form a new facade. It suits Kerala's heavy rain, humidity and strong sun when three things are right: an exterior-grade coating, stainless steel fixings and properly sealed joints.

Aluminium does not rust. Good exterior coatings resist UV fading. Most problems we see on old facades come from poor framing and open joints, not from the panel itself. That is why we detail drainage and sealing for the monsoon.

q: ACP vs HPL vs glass facade: which should I choose?
a:
Choose ACP for clean modern lines, a wide range of finishes and lighter weight. Choose HPL (high-pressure laminate) when you want a very realistic wood look and accept heavier panels. Choose glass where you need daylight and display, such as a showroom ground floor.

Many good facades combine them. A common pattern is glass at street level and ACP above. We explain the trade-offs for your building and budget, and compare them in our ACP vs HPL vs glass guide.

q: How long does an ACP facade last, and how do I maintain it?
a:
Service life depends mostly on the panel grade, the coating and the quality of installation. Ask for the manufacturer's coating warranty in writing for the exact panel used. [FILL: warranty FACADO offers on workmanship]

Maintenance is simple. Rinse with water and a mild detergent once or twice a year, more often near busy roads. Avoid abrasive pads and strong solvents. Check sealant joints after each monsoon.

q: Can you redo the facade of an old building without demolition?
a: Yes, in most cases. ACP is fixed on a framework anchored to the existing structure, so the old wall stays in place behind it. We first check the wall and structure during the site survey. If repairs are needed, such as loose plaster or leaks, we tell you before we design. Read more on facade renovation.

It depends on the core. Standard ACP has a polyethylene (PE) core, which is combustible. Fire-retardant (FR) panels use a mineral-filled core that resists burning much better. Panels with an even higher mineral content (often called A2 grade) are rated as limited-combustibility.

For high-rise buildings, hospitals, schools and other public buildings, we recommend FR or A2 cores and follow the applicable fire norms. Ask for the manufacturer's fire test certificate for the exact panel. We will always tell you which core we are quoting.
